title: Euclid’s view of globular cluster NGC 6397
caption: The globular cluster NGC 6397, imaged by ESA’s Euclid space telescope
celestial: NGC 6397 · constellation Ara · about 7,800 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi

recognition.text: One of Euclid’s first five full-color images (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A dense ball of stars sparkles at the center of this Euclid image, thinning into a wide halo at its edges. This is NGC 6397, a globular cluster about 7,800 light-years away in Ara, the Altar. It is the second-closest globular cluster to Earth.

Globular clusters are swarms of hundreds of thousands of stars bound together by gravity. They are among the oldest objects in the universe, so they hold clues to how galaxies like the Milky Way formed. NGC 6397 orbits our galaxy along with other globulars, around the disc where most of its stars live.

Capturing a whole globular cluster in one observation is usually difficult. The crowded core is so bright that its brightest stars drown out fainter ones, while the outskirts spread far and are made mostly of faint, low-mass stars. Those faint outer stars can reveal past run-ins with the Milky Way. Euclid caught both in about an hour.
scale: Using the source’s listed field of view (41 × 41 arcminutes) and the source’s distance of about 7,800 light-years, the frame spans roughly 93 × 93 light-years. Its light set out about 7,800 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Euclid combined its visible-light camera (VIS) with near-infrared measurements in the Y and H bands from its NISP instrument. Blue shows light at about 0.7 microns, green about 1.1 microns and red about 1.7 microns.
understand.eye: Two of the three colors are near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the mapping was chosen for looks: hot stars read white-blue and dusty regions red.

explore: In Euclid’s colors, hot stars look white-blue and distant galaxies in the background very red. The six spikes on bright stars come from diffraction in Euclid’s optics, and a few faint, fuzzy blue circles are “optical ghosts,” ordinary artifacts of a complex optical system that don’t affect the science.
alt: A dense, glittering ball of stars at center, spreading into thinner and thinner stars toward the edges of a dark field.
